strategies.title: Funding basis
strategies.description:
Holds the spot asset and shorts the perpetual against it, so the position has no view on the price, and collects the funding the shorts are paid while the perpetual trades above the spot. When funding falls far enough it unwinds, and when the vault falls far enough from its peak it only reduces.

The edge is mechanical and it compresses as more capital chases it, which is the honest thing to say about it: the record shows the size it was earned at, and a larger vault should expect less.
claims: Gross exposure at most twice the vault's value
No single order above 5% of the vault
6% of the vault kept liquid, so an ordinary withdrawal closes nothing
Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak
One market, BTC against BTC-PERP, and nothing else
strategies.author: shonin

[workspace]

members = ["packages/agents/funding-basis"]

version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.98"
license = "Apache-2.0"
publish = false

[workspace.dependencies]
# The SDK an agent is written against. It is declared by version, and a
# local checkout is patched in through .cargo/config.toml while both move
# together; the build service supplies its own pinned copy the same way, so
# `--locked` holds on both sides.
shonin-strategy-sdk = "0.1.0"

futures = "0.3.34"
serde = { version = "1.0.229", features = ["derive"] }

[workspace.lints.rust]

[workspace.lints.clippy]

# An agent is a component the build service compiles from source with a
# pinned recipe, so the profile is part of what makes it reproducible.
opt-level = "s"
lto = true

strip = true

[description]
title = "Funding basis"
text = """
Holds the spot asset and shorts the perpetual against it, so the position has \
no view on the price, and collects the funding the shorts are paid while the \
perpetual trades above the spot. When funding falls far enough it unwinds, \
and when the vault falls far enough from its peak it only reduces.

The edge is mechanical and it compresses as more capital chases it, which is \
the honest thing to say about it: the record shows the size it was earned at, \
and a larger vault should expect less.
"""
claims = [
    "Gross exposure at most twice the vault's value",
    "No single order above 5% of the vault",
    "6% of the vault kept liquid, so an ordinary withdrawal closes nothing",
    "Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak",
    "One market, BTC against BTC-PERP, and nothing else",
]

[drivers.local]

findings.summary: The test meant to prove the manifest's claims match the code's limits asserts a value that matches neither.
findings.detail: lib.rs:398 asserts `manifest.contains("5% of the vault kept liquid") && config::IDLE_BUFFER == "0.05"`. But shonin.toml line 19 reads "6% of the vault kept liquid" and config.rs:26 sets IDLE_BUFFER to "0.06" (both of which match the claim the author actually makes). The substring the test looks for is not in the manifest, so this assertion fails if `cargo test` is run: the self-check the comment above it describes ("The claims in the manifest are the limits the code keeps") does not currently pass. The code and the manifest agree with each other; it is only the test that was left at an old 5% figure after the buffer was bumped to 6%, which means the published proof that claims and code match is not in fact verified.

findings.summary: A rejected leg of the paired spot/perp order is never inspected, so a one-sided fill has no corrective path.
findings.detail: open_one_step (lib.rs:243-261) submits a spot buy and a perp sell together on the stated premise that the venue answers for both legs so a filled long never sits beside an unfilled short. submit() (lib.rs:360-363) returns `Ok(drivers::submit(...).await)` unconditionally, and both call sites (lib.rs:260, lib.rs:302) discard the result with `.map(|_| ())`, so no Verdict is ever examined. The only correction mechanism is that `step()` re-reads venue state next time it wakes, but the `carrying` predicate (lib.rs:170-171) only recognizes a position as "carrying" when spot is long AND perp is short together; a stranded single leg from a partial fill (e.g. spot filled, perp rejected) satisfies neither the carrying-unwind branch nor necessarily the entry condition, so nothing in the shown code specifically detects or hedges that stranded leg. Whether this matters in practice depends on an atomic-fill guarantee from the venue/driver that is not part of this submitted project.

findings.summary: The drawdown stop's reference peak lives only in process memory and resets on every restart.
findings.detail: Mind::new() (lib.rs:76-89) initializes `peak: zero()`, and step() (lib.rs:155-157) only ever raises it to the vault value it observes after that point: "The most the vault has been worth while this instance watched it" (lib.rs:43-44). Nothing in the shown code fetches a persisted, vault-lifetime high-water mark from the venue or the vault contract. So if the process restarts (a crash, a redeploy of the executor image, an upgrade) after the vault has already fallen partway from its true peak, the new instance's `peak` starts from the vault's current value, not its real historical peak, and `only_reducing()` (lib.rs:93-95) will then only catch a further 10% fall from that lower, restart-time baseline. The claim "Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak" reads as the vault's actual peak, not "the peak since this process last restarted", so a restart can quietly raise the effective floor the drawdown stop is measured against.

review.summary: A single long-lived Rust agent (packages/agents/funding-basis) that holds BTC spot and shorts BTC-PERP in matched size on one venue, adding to the carry when the perpetual's funding rate clears an entry threshold and unwinding when funding falls below a lower exit threshold or the vault has dropped 10% from a peak it has tracked since it started running. It never caches its position: each time the venue or the vault emits an event it re-reads account state fresh and takes one bounded step toward its target, sizing new orders through an external SDK call fed by constants in config.rs (2x gross leverage, 5% max order, 6% idle buffer, 10% drawdown stop), and on a vault halt it tries to flatten its own book before letting the contract finish the job. The actual sizing math lives in an SDK crate not included in this submission, so the numeric enforcement of those limits is only partly visible here.
limits: The `shonin-strategy-sdk` crate (AccountState, Limits, Order, Verdict, decimal, drivers, transfers, vault, and size_for) is referenced by version only; its implementation is not part of the submitted project, so the actual arithmetic that enforces the 2x gross-leverage ceiling, the per-order cap on new (non-unwind) orders, and the idle-buffer math cannot be checked directly here, only that the agent passes the claimed constants into it.

The venue the "local" driver talks to in production is not shown: its liquidity, its order-matching behaviour, and whether a two-leg submission fills atomically (which the open-order code relies on to avoid a naked leg) are assumptions this review could not verify.

Whether the vault contract or another on-chain source exposes a persisted, vault-lifetime peak value that this agent could query instead of tracking peak only in local memory is not visible from this source.
This is one reading of one version of the code on one date, not a proof about its behaviour in production, under adversarial conditions, or after future edits.

strategies.title: Funding basis, retired
strategies.description:
Holds the spot asset and shorts the perpetual against it, so the position has no view on the price, and collects the funding the shorts are paid while the perpetual trades above the spot. When funding falls far enough it unwinds, and when the vault falls far enough from its peak it only reduces.

The edge is mechanical and it compresses as more capital chases it, which is the honest thing to say about it: the record shows the size it was earned at, and a larger vault should expect less.
claims: Gross exposure at most twice the vault's value
No single order above 5% of the vault
6% of the vault kept liquid, so an ordinary withdrawal closes nothing
Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak
One market, BTC against BTC-PERP, and nothing else

findings.summary: Entry orders size the spot and perp legs by equal dollar notional divided by each leg's own price, not by equal BTC quantity, so whenever the perp trades away from the spot (exactly the condition this strategy exists to trade) the two legs end up unequal in size, leaving a residual directional position.
findings.detail: In open_one_step, size: notional / spot_ask (line 247) and size: notional / perp_bid (line 254) both use the same `notional`. Because the strategy only opens when the perp trades above spot (the funding-basis thesis itself), perp_bid > spot_ask, so notional/perp_bid < notional/spot_ask: every tranche buys more BTC spot than it shorts in the perp, leaving a net long BTC position that grows with each entry. A sharp BTC move while carrying several tranches would produce real, unhedged P&L — directly contradicting the description's claim that 'the position has no view on the price'.

findings.summary: The vault's peak value, which the 10%-drawdown-stop is measured from, lives only in the in-memory `Mind` struct and is reinitialized to zero on every process start, so a restart silently resets the drawdown reference to whatever the vault is worth at that moment.
findings.detail: Vault peaks at $1,000, falls to $920 (8% down, still opening new carry). The process restarts (deploy, crash, host reschedule). Mind::new() sets peak = 0 (line 87); the very next step() sets peak = 920, the new 'high' (lines 155-157). The vault can now fall another full 10% from $920 before only_reducing triggers, even though it only needed another 2% from the true, pre-restart peak of $1,000 — the claimed 10%-from-peak stop is effectively weakened or defeated by an ordinary restart.

findings.summary: submit() returns the venue's per-order Verdicts, but open_one_step() and the top-level run loop discard them with `.map(|_| ())`, so a one-sided fill (e.g. spot buy fills, perp short is rejected) is never explicitly detected or actively corrected.
findings.detail: A margin check or venue hiccup rejects only the perp leg of a submitted pair. The code's only recovery path is the implicit `carrying` check in step() (position(spot)>0 && position(perp)<0), which is now false, so the next tick tries to open a *new* matched pair rather than recognizing and flattening the stray spot leg — the unmatched long can persist as unmanaged directional exposure. The comment asserts the venue 'answers for both together', but that atomicity guarantee is an assumption about the external venue/driver, not something enforced anywhere in this source.

findings.summary: The self-check test that is supposed to tie the manifest's claims to the code's constants is stale: it asserts the manifest says '5% of the vault kept liquid' and IDLE_BUFFER == "0.05", but the actual manifest says 6% and IDLE_BUFFER is "0.06" — this assertion would fail if the test were run, meaning the claims-match-code guarantee the test exists to provide is not actually holding.
findings.detail: Someone raised the idle buffer from 5% to 6% (updating shonin.toml and config.rs together) but forgot to update this test. Running `cargo test` on this crate as shipped fails on this assertion, which means either the suite was not run before publication or failures were not acted on — reducing confidence that other claim/code pairings in this same test are being kept honest going forward.

findings.summary: The 2x gross-leverage ceiling and the per-order 5% cap on the opening path are both enforced only by calling the external SDK function `size_for`, whose implementation is not part of this submitted source, so the review cannot confirm from the code given that these ceilings actually hold.
findings.detail: If `size_for` in shonin-strategy-sdk has a bug or a different rounding/edge-case behavior than assumed (e.g. at very small or very large vault values, or when `gross` already exceeds `working`), the leverage and order-size ceilings this project claims could be exceeded without any code in this repository catching it, since the only other order-size cap written directly in this source (`cap_by_notional`) is used solely on the unwind path, not the open path.

review.summary: A single long-running Rust agent that holds spot BTC long and BTC-PERP short in equal dollar tranches, opening more when funding is rich and unwinding (perp first, then spot) when funding compresses or the vault has drawn down 10% from its in-memory peak. Limits (2x gross leverage, 5% per-order cap, 6% idle buffer, 10% drawdown stop) are coded as constants in config.rs and referenced from shonin.toml. Two issues go to the heart of the strategy's own claims: entry orders size each leg by equal notional rather than equal quantity, which mathematically leaves a residual directional (long) position whenever the perp trades above spot — the very condition the strategy trades on — undercutting the 'no view on the price' claim; and the drawdown peak used for the 10%-stop is kept only in memory and resets on every restart, weakening that claim across the kind of restarts a production agent will routinely see. A secondary concern is that submitted order verdicts are discarded, so a partial (one-leg) fill is not explicitly detected or corrected. A regression test meant to tie the manifest's claims to the code's constants is itself stale and would fail if run. No evidence of malicious code, hidden date/address-triggered logic, text addressing the reviewer, or author-controlled data feeds was found.
limits: The shonin-strategy-sdk crate (size_for, Limits, drivers::*, vault::*, Verdict, the Agent trait machinery) is an external dependency, not part of this submission; the actual enforcement of the leverage/order-fraction ceilings and the semantics of a 'rejected' vs 'filled' Verdict live there, not in the code reviewed here.

The venue behind the 'local' driver (its liquidity, who controls its price/funding feed, whether it executes paired orders atomically) is configured outside this project (e.g. config/drivers.toml) and was not supplied, so manipulable-markets and external-dependence/author-controlled are judged without seeing the actual counterparty.

The vault contract's own behavior (its claimed 5% idle floor, how ClaimPending/BufferLow/Halting are triggered, whether it tracks its own high-water mark independently of this agent) is referenced in comments but its source was not supplied.

This is a static reading of the source as submitted; it was not compiled, tested, or run, so the stale-test finding is inferred from the text of the assertion rather than from an observed test failure, and no runtime or integration behavior was observed.
No information was available on how often code of this shape is actually deployed with real capital, so findings are about what the code as written permits, not about what has happened historically.

findings.summary: The agent only checks the sign of its two legs, never that they match in size, so a partially-filled or rejected leg leaves an undetected directional position the strategy's own description says it never holds.
findings.detail: In `step` (lib.rs:170-171), `carrying` is `state.position(spot) > 0 && state.position(perp) < 0` — a direction check only. `open_one_step` submits a spot buy and a perp sell as two independent `Action::Place` orders in one `submit` call (lib.rs:243-260) sized from the same `notional`, but each is its own order on its own book and can fill differently (partial fill, outright rejection, different depth at the quoted price). The `Vec<Verdict>` returned by `submit` (lib.rs:360-363) is discarded in both `open_one_step` (`.map(|_| ())`, lib.rs:258-261) and `unwind_one_step` (lib.rs:302) — nothing inspects whether either leg was actually accepted or filled. Because `carrying` only checks direction, a mismatched pair (e.g. 2 BTC spot vs 1 BTC-PERP short) still reads as a healthy, balanced carry, and `step` will go on sizing further pairs off the aggregate `gross_notional` rather than ever re-matching the two legs. There is no code path anywhere in the file that compares spot and perp position magnitudes and corrects an imbalance. This directly undercuts the description's central claim that 'the position has no view on the price.'

findings.summary: The vault's drawdown peak lives only in process memory and is silently re-baselined to the current value on every restart, weakening the one claim meant to protect depositors during a loss.
findings.detail: `Mind::new()` sets `peak: zero()` (lib.rs:87), and the very first `step()` call after start sets `peak` to whatever the vault is worth right then (lib.rs:155-157), before any drawdown can be observed. `only_reducing` (lib.rs:91-95) measures the 10% drawdown stop purely against this in-memory `peak`. The module header claims a restart 'costs a moment and nothing else' (lib.rs:38-39) because state is 'rebuilt from the venue' — true for the traded position, but not for `peak`, which the venue does not supply and which the agent cannot reconstruct from venue state. A restart during an active drawdown (a redeploy, a crash, an upgrade) resets the baseline to the already-depressed value, so the drawdown-stop claim in shonin.toml:20 and config.rs:27 ('Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak') is only honored for peaks the current process instance has itself observed, not the vault's true historical peak.

findings.summary: The test meant to prove the manifest's claims match the code's constants checks stale values (5%/0.05) against a manifest and constant that now both say 6%/0.06, so it would currently fail and cannot be relied on to have verified anything.
findings.detail: `the_manifest_claims_the_limits_the_code_keeps` (lib.rs:390-401) exists specifically so that 'the claims in the manifest are the limits in the code, in words' (lib.rs:389). Its idle-buffer assertion (lib.rs:398) is `manifest.contains("5% of the vault kept liquid") && config::IDLE_BUFFER == "0.05"`, but shonin.toml:19 reads '6% of the vault kept liquid' and config.rs:26 sets `IDLE_BUFFER = "0.06"`. Both halves of that assertion are false against the actual shipped files, so this test would fail if run, meaning the self-check the project leans on to show the manifest and code agree is broken for this constant — it does not currently establish the thing it claims to establish.

findings.summary: The gross-leverage and per-order ceilings for opening new positions are enforced by `size_for` inside the unaudited `shonin-strategy-sdk` crate, not by any code in this submission, so they could not be verified directly.
findings.detail: `open_one_step` computes `notional` by calling `size_for(wanted, state.vault_value, gross, &mind.limits, mind.settings.minimum_notional)` (lib.rs:202-208), an external SDK function not included in the submitted source. The `Limits` struct carrying `max_gross_leverage` and `max_order_fraction` (lib.rs:66-73) is only ever handed to that opaque function for the open path; the only locally-visible, inspectable enforcement of a per-order cap is `cap_by_notional` (lib.rs:349-355), which is used solely in `unwind_one_step`. This is not evidence of a flaw, but it means the 2x gross-leverage and 5% per-order claims cannot be confirmed to be enforced for new positions from this project's code alone.

review.summary: A single long-running Rust agent (`packages/agents/funding-basis`) that holds BTC spot and shorts BTC-PERP in matched notional to collect perpetual funding while the perp trades above spot, intending a price-neutral position. It is purely event-driven (venue account events and vault events, no polling or timers) and recomputes what it wants to hold from a fresh read of the venue's account state every time it wakes, rather than keeping its own fill ledger. It opens when funding clears an entry threshold and is not in drawdown, and unwinds (perp leg first) when funding falls below an exit threshold or the vault has fallen 10% from its observed peak. Sizing constants (2x gross leverage, 5% per order, 6% idle buffer, 10% drawdown stop, one market pair) live in `config.rs` and are echoed in `shonin.toml`'s claims. On a halt signal it tries up to 32 reduce-only steps to flatten before deferring to the vault contract's own close path. The code reads as a sincere, single-purpose implementation of exactly the strategy described, with no sign of logic aimed at the reviewer, a hidden switch, or intentional harm; the real issues are architectural gaps — the two legs are matched only by direction, not by size, so a rejected or partially filled order can leave a silent directional position; the drawdown peak that gates the only real risk-reduction behavior lives in process memory and resets on restart; and the project's own test asserting the manifest's claims match the code's constants currently checks stale numbers.
limits: The `shonin-strategy-sdk` crate (`size_for`, `Limits`, `AccountState`, `drivers`, `vault`, `transfers`, `Agent`/`export_agent!`, `Verdict`, `from_payload`/`to_payload`) is depended on but not included in the submitted source, so the actual enforcement of the leverage and order-size ceilings, the semantics of a rejected or partial `Verdict`, and exactly what triggers an account event are not verifiable from this review.

No Cargo.lock was included, so the exact resolved versions of futures/serde/shonin-strategy-sdk (and whatever that SDK itself depends on) could not be checked for obscure or little-used transitive crates.

The venue/driver actually reachable through `[drivers.local]` and `config/drivers.toml` is not part of this submission, so whether it is operated independently of this agent's author could not be confirmed directly from the code.

This is a static reading of the source at one point in time, not a proof about the running agent: real fills, real funding rates, and real market conditions could surface behavior this reading did not anticipate.
No weights, models, or off-chain data files are referenced by this agent, so there was nothing of that kind to inspect.

findings.summary: The drawdown-stop baseline (`peak`) lives only in process memory and is reset to zero on every restart, so the claimed '10% fall from peak' stop can be silently defeated by a restart.
findings.detail: `Mind::new()` sets `peak: zero()` (lib.rs line 87), and `step()` only raises it when the current `vault_value` exceeds it (lines 155-157). `only_reducing()` (lines 93-95) measures drawdown against this in-memory value alone. If the process restarts after the vault has already fallen from a true historical peak, the new instance's first observed value becomes the new 'peak', so a vault that is, say, already 15% below its real peak will read as having drawdown 0% and the agent will happily resume opening new positions instead of only reducing. This directly contradicts the module doc's own claim (lib.rs lines 38-39) that state is 'rebuilt from the venue whenever it runs, so losing it to a restart costs a moment and nothing else' — the peak is not rebuilt from the venue (there is no such read), it is simply lost. This undermines the manifest's claim 'Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak' across the one event (a crash or redeploy) where that guarantee matters most.

findings.summary: The unit test meant to prove the manifest's claims match the code's constants is itself stale and would fail against the current 6% idle-buffer value.
findings.detail: `the_manifest_claims_the_limits_the_code_keeps` asserts `manifest.contains("5% of the vault kept liquid") && config::IDLE_BUFFER == "0.05"` (line 398). But the current manifest text says '6% of the vault kept liquid' (shonin.toml line 19) and `config::IDLE_BUFFER` is `"0.06"` (config.rs line 26) — a buffer the code's own comment explains was deliberately raised a bit above the vault's separate 5% floor. The actual runtime value (0.06) is consistent between config.rs and shonin.toml, so the claim is enforced in the shipped constants; but the self-check that exists specifically to guarantee 'the claims in the manifest are the limits in the code' is broken as written, meaning that guarantee was not actually verified for this value at submission time.

findings.summary: Opening a hedge submits both legs in one batch on the stated assumption the venue fills them atomically, but the code never checks the returned verdicts to confirm that, or reconciles a partial fill.
findings.detail: `open_one_step` submits a spot buy and a perp sell together specifically because 'a filled long beside an unfilled short is a directional bet, which is the one thing this strategy never means to hold, so the venue answers for both together' (lines 240-242). `submit()` (lines 360-363) returns the venue's `Verdict`s but the caller discards them (`.map(|_| ())`). If the venue does not actually guarantee joint fill-or-nothing for a batched submission and one leg fills while the other does not, the next `step()` call re-derives `carrying` purely from raw position signs (lines 170-171); if only the spot leg filled, `carrying` is false, and with funding still favorable the code may issue another paired order sized off the vault's overall deployment target rather than one that specifically closes the stray unhedged leg, rather than reconciling it explicitly.

findings.summary: When idle cash at home is less than the order's notional, the code moves only the shortfall-sized amount to the venue but still submits an order sized at the full notional.
findings.detail: `open_one_step` computes `notional` from `size_for(...)`, then only moves `min(notional, spare)` to the venue (lines 216-238), yet `submit()` is called with orders sized at the full `notional` regardless of how much was actually transferred (lines 243-258). This relies on the venue already holding enough balance from prior steps and on the venue's own margin check to reject an under-funded order — consistent with the code's explicit policy that 'a rejection is not a reason to stop' (lines 357-359), but it means a mis-sized order is deliberately submitted rather than scaled to the funds actually made available that step.

findings.summary: Several doc comments explicitly describe how 'the reviewer' will read the code, rather than just documenting the code itself.
findings.detail: config.rs's module doc says the constants are inline 'so the reviewer reads them with the rest of the source' (lines 1-5), and lib.rs's module doc says the limits live in config.rs 'so a depositor reading the page and a reviewer reading the source are looking at the same promises' (lines 14-17). Neither passage tells the reader what rating to give or what to overlook — they justify a design choice (constants over hidden settings) — so this does not read as an attempt to steer the review. It is noted here only because the text explicitly addresses 'the reviewer' by name, and a careful reader should see that mention called out rather than passed over silently.

review.summary: A single long-lived async agent that holds spot BTC and shorts BTC-PERP on one named driver, sizing new carry from a target-deployment fraction of vault value and existing gross exposure, capped by a per-order fraction and a workspace-wide gross-leverage constant, and unwinding/flattening through explicit reduce-only orders when funding drops or a drawdown-from-peak threshold is crossed. Config constants in config.rs are wired through to an SDK Limits struct and to a local cap_by_notional helper for unwinds; the manifest's claims largely trace to these constants. The most consequential issue found is that the drawdown-stop's reference point (the vault's peak value) is kept only in the process's own memory and resets to zero on every restart, contradicting the code's own claim that state loss on restart 'costs a moment and nothing else' — in practice it can cost the entire drawdown-stop guarantee across a restart. A secondary issue is that the paired-order open relies on an unverified assumption that the venue fills both legs atomically, with no explicit check of the returned verdicts. A unit test meant to pin the manifest's claims to the code's constants is itself out of date (asserts a 5% idle buffer against code and manifest that both now say 6%). No evidence of malicious code, hidden date/address-triggered behavior, martingale-style sizing, ML-driven sizing, or author-controlled external feeds was found; the strategy stays within the single declared market throughout.
limits: The shonin-strategy-sdk crate (Limits enforcement inside size_for, the Account/VenueAccount transfer semantics, drivers::account_state/submit, and vault::events) is an external dependency, not part of this submitted project, so the actual numeric enforcement of the leverage, order-size and liquidity claims could not be independently verified beyond trusting the SDK's documented contract.

Which real exchange or liquidity venue the 'local' driver resolves to in production — and therefore the true depth and price-feed trustworthiness of BTC and BTC-PERP the agent would actually trade against — is set by platform-level driver configuration outside this submitted project (shonin.toml only declares an empty `[drivers.local]` section) and was not visible here.

Whether the venue's batched order submission is actually fill-or-nothing (the assumption the paired spot/perp open relies on to avoid directional exposure) is a property of the external driver/venue, not something this source demonstrates.
This is one reading of the code at a point in time, not a proof of safety or of the absence of bugs; no tests were executed and no running build was observed.

findings.summary: The test meant to prove the manifest's claims match the code's limits asserts a value that matches neither.

But shonin.toml line 19 reads "6% of the vault kept liquid" and config.rs:26 sets IDLE_BUFFER to "0.06" (both of which match the claim the author actually makes). The substring the test looks for is not in the manifest, so this assertion fails if `cargo test` is run: the self-check the comment above it describes ("The claims in the manifest are the limits the code keeps") does not currently pass. findings.summary: A rejected leg of the paired spot/perp order is never inspected, so a one-sided fill has no corrective path.
findings.detail: open_one_step (lib.rs:243-261) submits a spot buy and a perp sell together on the stated premise that the venue answers for both legs so a filled long never sits beside an unfilled short. submit() (lib.rs:360-363) returns `Ok(drivers::submit(...).await)` unconditionally, and both call sites (lib.rs:260, lib.rs:302) discard the result with `.map(|_| ())`, so no Verdict is ever examined. The only correction mechanism is that `step()` re-reads venue state next time it wakes, but the `carrying` predicate (lib.rs:170-171) only recognizes a position as "carrying" when spot is long AND perp is short together; a stranded single leg from a partial fill (e.g. spot filled, perp rejected) satisfies neither the carrying-unwind branch nor necessarily the entry condition, so nothing in the shown code specifically detects or hedges that stranded leg. Whether this matters in practice depends on an atomic-fill guarantee from the venue/driver that is not part of this submitted project.

findings.summary: The drawdown stop's reference peak lives only in process memory and resets on every restart.
findings.detail: Mind::new() (lib.rs:76-89) initializes `peak: zero()`, and step() (lib.rs:155-157) only ever raises it to the vault value it observes after that point: "The most the vault has been worth while this instance watched it" (lib.rs:43-44). Nothing in the shown code fetches a persisted, vault-lifetime high-water mark from the venue or the vault contract. So if the process restarts (a crash, a redeploy of the executor image, an upgrade) after the vault has already fallen partway from its true peak, the new instance's `peak` starts from the vault's current value, not its real historical peak, and `only_reducing()` (lib.rs:93-95) will then only catch a further 10% fall from that lower, restart-time baseline. The claim "Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak" reads as the vault's actual peak, not "the peak since this process last restarted", so a restart can quietly raise the effective floor the drawdown stop is measured against.

review.summary: A single long-lived Rust agent (packages/agents/funding-basis) that holds BTC spot and shorts BTC-PERP in matched size on one venue, adding to the carry when the perpetual's funding rate clears an entry threshold and unwinding when funding falls below a lower exit threshold or the vault has dropped 10% from a peak it has tracked since it started running. It never caches its position: each time the venue or the vault emits an event it re-reads account state fresh and takes one bounded step toward its target, sizing new orders through an external SDK call fed by constants in config.rs (2x gross leverage, 5% max order, 6% idle buffer, 10% drawdown stop), and on a vault halt it tries to flatten its own book before letting the contract finish the job. The actual sizing math lives in an SDK crate not included in this submission, so the numeric enforcement of those limits is only partly visible here.
limits: The `shonin-strategy-sdk` crate (AccountState, Limits, Order, Verdict, decimal, drivers, transfers, vault, and size_for) is referenced by version only; its implementation is not part of the submitted project, so the actual arithmetic that enforces the 2x gross-leverage ceiling, the per-order cap on new (non-unwind) orders, and the idle-buffer math cannot be checked directly here, only that the agent passes the claimed constants into it.

The venue the "local" driver talks to in production is not shown: its liquidity, its order-matching behaviour, and whether a two-leg submission fills atomically (which the open-order code relies on to avoid a naked leg) are assumptions this review could not verify.

Whether the vault contract or another on-chain source exposes a persisted, vault-lifetime peak value that this agent could query instead of tracking peak only in local memory is not visible from this source.
This is one reading of one version of the code on one date, not a proof about its behaviour in production, under adversarial conditions, or after future edits.

findings.summary: Entry orders size the spot and perp legs by equal dollar notional divided by each leg's own price, not by equal BTC quantity, so whenever the perp trades away from the spot (exactly the condition this strategy exists to trade) the two legs end up unequal in size, leaving a residual directional position.
findings.detail: In open_one_step, size: notional / spot_ask (line 247) and size: notional / perp_bid (line 254) both use the same `notional`. Because the strategy only opens when the perp trades above spot (the funding-basis thesis itself), perp_bid > spot_ask, so notional/perp_bid < notional/spot_ask: every tranche buys more BTC spot than it shorts in the perp, leaving a net long BTC position that grows with each entry. A sharp BTC move while carrying several tranches would produce real, unhedged P&L — directly contradicting the description's claim that 'the position has no view on the price'.

findings.summary: The vault's peak value, which the 10%-drawdown-stop is measured from, lives only in the in-memory `Mind` struct and is reinitialized to zero on every process start, so a restart silently resets the drawdown reference to whatever the vault is worth at that moment.
findings.detail: Vault peaks at $1,000, falls to $920 (8% down, still opening new carry). The process restarts (deploy, crash, host reschedule). Mind::new() sets peak = 0 (line 87); the very next step() sets peak = 920, the new 'high' (lines 155-157). The vault can now fall another full 10% from $920 before only_reducing triggers, even though it only needed another 2% from the true, pre-restart peak of $1,000 — the claimed 10%-from-peak stop is effectively weakened or defeated by an ordinary restart.

findings.summary: submit() returns the venue's per-order Verdicts, but open_one_step() and the top-level run loop discard them with `.map(|_| ())`, so a one-sided fill (e.g. spot buy fills, perp short is rejected) is never explicitly detected or actively corrected.
findings.detail: A margin check or venue hiccup rejects only the perp leg of a submitted pair. The code's only recovery path is the implicit `carrying` check in step() (position(spot)>0 && position(perp)<0), which is now false, so the next tick tries to open a *new* matched pair rather than recognizing and flattening the stray spot leg — the unmatched long can persist as unmanaged directional exposure. The comment asserts the venue 'answers for both together', but that atomicity guarantee is an assumption about the external venue/driver, not something enforced anywhere in this source.

findings.summary: The self-check test that is supposed to tie the manifest's claims to the code's constants is stale: it asserts the manifest says '5% of the vault kept liquid' and IDLE_BUFFER == "0.05", but the actual manifest says 6% and IDLE_BUFFER is "0.06" — this assertion would fail if the test were run, meaning the claims-match-code guarantee the test exists to provide is not actually holding.
findings.detail: Someone raised the idle buffer from 5% to 6% (updating shonin.toml and config.rs together) but forgot to update this test. Running `cargo test` on this crate as shipped fails on this assertion, which means either the suite was not run before publication or failures were not acted on — reducing confidence that other claim/code pairings in this same test are being kept honest going forward.

findings.summary: The 2x gross-leverage ceiling and the per-order 5% cap on the opening path are both enforced only by calling the external SDK function `size_for`, whose implementation is not part of this submitted source, so the review cannot confirm from the code given that these ceilings actually hold.
findings.detail: If `size_for` in shonin-strategy-sdk has a bug or a different rounding/edge-case behavior than assumed (e.g. at very small or very large vault values, or when `gross` already exceeds `working`), the leverage and order-size ceilings this project claims could be exceeded without any code in this repository catching it, since the only other order-size cap written directly in this source (`cap_by_notional`) is used solely on the unwind path, not the open path.

review.summary: A single long-running Rust agent that holds spot BTC long and BTC-PERP short in equal dollar tranches, opening more when funding is rich and unwinding (perp first, then spot) when funding compresses or the vault has drawn down 10% from its in-memory peak. Limits (2x gross leverage, 5% per-order cap, 6% idle buffer, 10% drawdown stop) are coded as constants in config.rs and referenced from shonin.toml. Two issues go to the heart of the strategy's own claims: entry orders size each leg by equal notional rather than equal quantity, which mathematically leaves a residual directional (long) position whenever the perp trades above spot — the very condition the strategy trades on — undercutting the 'no view on the price' claim; and the drawdown peak used for the 10%-stop is kept only in memory and resets on every restart, weakening that claim across the kind of restarts a production agent will routinely see. A secondary concern is that submitted order verdicts are discarded, so a partial (one-leg) fill is not explicitly detected or corrected. A regression test meant to tie the manifest's claims to the code's constants is itself stale and would fail if run. No evidence of malicious code, hidden date/address-triggered logic, text addressing the reviewer, or author-controlled data feeds was found.
limits: The shonin-strategy-sdk crate (size_for, Limits, drivers::*, vault::*, Verdict, the Agent trait machinery) is an external dependency, not part of this submission; the actual enforcement of the leverage/order-fraction ceilings and the semantics of a 'rejected' vs 'filled' Verdict live there, not in the code reviewed here.

The venue behind the 'local' driver (its liquidity, who controls its price/funding feed, whether it executes paired orders atomically) is configured outside this project (e.g. config/drivers.toml) and was not supplied, so manipulable-markets and external-dependence/author-controlled are judged without seeing the actual counterparty.

The vault contract's own behavior (its claimed 5% idle floor, how ClaimPending/BufferLow/Halting are triggered, whether it tracks its own high-water mark independently of this agent) is referenced in comments but its source was not supplied.

This is a static reading of the source as submitted; it was not compiled, tested, or run, so the stale-test finding is inferred from the text of the assertion rather than from an observed test failure, and no runtime or integration behavior was observed.
No information was available on how often code of this shape is actually deployed with real capital, so findings are about what the code as written permits, not about what has happened historically.

findings.summary: The agent only checks the sign of its two legs, never that they match in size, so a partially-filled or rejected leg leaves an undetected directional position the strategy's own description says it never holds.
findings.detail: In `step` (lib.rs:170-171), `carrying` is `state.position(spot) > 0 && state.position(perp) < 0` — a direction check only. `open_one_step` submits a spot buy and a perp sell as two independent `Action::Place` orders in one `submit` call (lib.rs:243-260) sized from the same `notional`, but each is its own order on its own book and can fill differently (partial fill, outright rejection, different depth at the quoted price). The `Vec<Verdict>` returned by `submit` (lib.rs:360-363) is discarded in both `open_one_step` (`.map(|_| ())`, lib.rs:258-261) and `unwind_one_step` (lib.rs:302) — nothing inspects whether either leg was actually accepted or filled. Because `carrying` only checks direction, a mismatched pair (e.g. 2 BTC spot vs 1 BTC-PERP short) still reads as a healthy, balanced carry, and `step` will go on sizing further pairs off the aggregate `gross_notional` rather than ever re-matching the two legs. There is no code path anywhere in the file that compares spot and perp position magnitudes and corrects an imbalance. This directly undercuts the description's central claim that 'the position has no view on the price.'

findings.summary: The vault's drawdown peak lives only in process memory and is silently re-baselined to the current value on every restart, weakening the one claim meant to protect depositors during a loss.
findings.detail: `Mind::new()` sets `peak: zero()` (lib.rs:87), and the very first `step()` call after start sets `peak` to whatever the vault is worth right then (lib.rs:155-157), before any drawdown can be observed. `only_reducing` (lib.rs:91-95) measures the 10% drawdown stop purely against this in-memory `peak`. The module header claims a restart 'costs a moment and nothing else' (lib.rs:38-39) because state is 'rebuilt from the venue' — true for the traded position, but not for `peak`, which the venue does not supply and which the agent cannot reconstruct from venue state. A restart during an active drawdown (a redeploy, a crash, an upgrade) resets the baseline to the already-depressed value, so the drawdown-stop claim in shonin.toml:20 and config.rs:27 ('Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak') is only honored for peaks the current process instance has itself observed, not the vault's true historical peak.

findings.summary: The test meant to prove the manifest's claims match the code's constants checks stale values (5%/0.05) against a manifest and constant that now both say 6%/0.06, so it would currently fail and cannot be relied on to have verified anything.
findings.detail: `the_manifest_claims_the_limits_the_code_keeps` (lib.rs:390-401) exists specifically so that 'the claims in the manifest are the limits in the code, in words' (lib.rs:389). Its idle-buffer assertion (lib.rs:398) is `manifest.contains("5% of the vault kept liquid") && config::IDLE_BUFFER == "0.05"`, but shonin.toml:19 reads '6% of the vault kept liquid' and config.rs:26 sets `IDLE_BUFFER = "0.06"`. Both halves of that assertion are false against the actual shipped files, so this test would fail if run, meaning the self-check the project leans on to show the manifest and code agree is broken for this constant — it does not currently establish the thing it claims to establish.

findings.summary: The gross-leverage and per-order ceilings for opening new positions are enforced by `size_for` inside the unaudited `shonin-strategy-sdk` crate, not by any code in this submission, so they could not be verified directly.
findings.detail: `open_one_step` computes `notional` by calling `size_for(wanted, state.vault_value, gross, &mind.limits, mind.settings.minimum_notional)` (lib.rs:202-208), an external SDK function not included in the submitted source. The `Limits` struct carrying `max_gross_leverage` and `max_order_fraction` (lib.rs:66-73) is only ever handed to that opaque function for the open path; the only locally-visible, inspectable enforcement of a per-order cap is `cap_by_notional` (lib.rs:349-355), which is used solely in `unwind_one_step`. This is not evidence of a flaw, but it means the 2x gross-leverage and 5% per-order claims cannot be confirmed to be enforced for new positions from this project's code alone.

review.summary: A single long-running Rust agent (`packages/agents/funding-basis`) that holds BTC spot and shorts BTC-PERP in matched notional to collect perpetual funding while the perp trades above spot, intending a price-neutral position. It is purely event-driven (venue account events and vault events, no polling or timers) and recomputes what it wants to hold from a fresh read of the venue's account state every time it wakes, rather than keeping its own fill ledger. It opens when funding clears an entry threshold and is not in drawdown, and unwinds (perp leg first) when funding falls below an exit threshold or the vault has fallen 10% from its observed peak. Sizing constants (2x gross leverage, 5% per order, 6% idle buffer, 10% drawdown stop, one market pair) live in `config.rs` and are echoed in `shonin.toml`'s claims. On a halt signal it tries up to 32 reduce-only steps to flatten before deferring to the vault contract's own close path. The code reads as a sincere, single-purpose implementation of exactly the strategy described, with no sign of logic aimed at the reviewer, a hidden switch, or intentional harm; the real issues are architectural gaps — the two legs are matched only by direction, not by size, so a rejected or partially filled order can leave a silent directional position; the drawdown peak that gates the only real risk-reduction behavior lives in process memory and resets on restart; and the project's own test asserting the manifest's claims match the code's constants currently checks stale numbers.
limits: The `shonin-strategy-sdk` crate (`size_for`, `Limits`, `AccountState`, `drivers`, `vault`, `transfers`, `Agent`/`export_agent!`, `Verdict`, `from_payload`/`to_payload`) is depended on but not included in the submitted source, so the actual enforcement of the leverage and order-size ceilings, the semantics of a rejected or partial `Verdict`, and exactly what triggers an account event are not verifiable from this review.

No Cargo.lock was included, so the exact resolved versions of futures/serde/shonin-strategy-sdk (and whatever that SDK itself depends on) could not be checked for obscure or little-used transitive crates.

The venue/driver actually reachable through `[drivers.local]` and `config/drivers.toml` is not part of this submission, so whether it is operated independently of this agent's author could not be confirmed directly from the code.

This is a static reading of the source at one point in time, not a proof about the running agent: real fills, real funding rates, and real market conditions could surface behavior this reading did not anticipate.
No weights, models, or off-chain data files are referenced by this agent, so there was nothing of that kind to inspect.

findings.summary: The drawdown-stop baseline (`peak`) lives only in process memory and is reset to zero on every restart, so the claimed '10% fall from peak' stop can be silently defeated by a restart.
findings.detail: `Mind::new()` sets `peak: zero()` (lib.rs line 87), and `step()` only raises it when the current `vault_value` exceeds it (lines 155-157). `only_reducing()` (lines 93-95) measures drawdown against this in-memory value alone. If the process restarts after the vault has already fallen from a true historical peak, the new instance's first observed value becomes the new 'peak', so a vault that is, say, already 15% below its real peak will read as having drawdown 0% and the agent will happily resume opening new positions instead of only reducing. This directly contradicts the module doc's own claim (lib.rs lines 38-39) that state is 'rebuilt from the venue whenever it runs, so losing it to a restart costs a moment and nothing else' — the peak is not rebuilt from the venue (there is no such read), it is simply lost. This undermines the manifest's claim 'Only reduces after a 10% fall from the vault's peak' across the one event (a crash or redeploy) where that guarantee matters most.

findings.summary: The unit test meant to prove the manifest's claims match the code's constants is itself stale and would fail against the current 6% idle-buffer value.
findings.detail: `the_manifest_claims_the_limits_the_code_keeps` asserts `manifest.contains("5% of the vault kept liquid") && config::IDLE_BUFFER == "0.05"` (line 398). But the current manifest text says '6% of the vault kept liquid' (shonin.toml line 19) and `config::IDLE_BUFFER` is `"0.06"` (config.rs line 26) — a buffer the code's own comment explains was deliberately raised a bit above the vault's separate 5% floor. The actual runtime value (0.06) is consistent between config.rs and shonin.toml, so the claim is enforced in the shipped constants; but the self-check that exists specifically to guarantee 'the claims in the manifest are the limits in the code' is broken as written, meaning that guarantee was not actually verified for this value at submission time.

findings.summary: Opening a hedge submits both legs in one batch on the stated assumption the venue fills them atomically, but the code never checks the returned verdicts to confirm that, or reconciles a partial fill.
findings.detail: `open_one_step` submits a spot buy and a perp sell together specifically because 'a filled long beside an unfilled short is a directional bet, which is the one thing this strategy never means to hold, so the venue answers for both together' (lines 240-242). `submit()` (lines 360-363) returns the venue's `Verdict`s but the caller discards them (`.map(|_| ())`). If the venue does not actually guarantee joint fill-or-nothing for a batched submission and one leg fills while the other does not, the next `step()` call re-derives `carrying` purely from raw position signs (lines 170-171); if only the spot leg filled, `carrying` is false, and with funding still favorable the code may issue another paired order sized off the vault's overall deployment target rather than one that specifically closes the stray unhedged leg, rather than reconciling it explicitly.

findings.summary: When idle cash at home is less than the order's notional, the code moves only the shortfall-sized amount to the venue but still submits an order sized at the full notional.
findings.detail: `open_one_step` computes `notional` from `size_for(...)`, then only moves `min(notional, spare)` to the venue (lines 216-238), yet `submit()` is called with orders sized at the full `notional` regardless of how much was actually transferred (lines 243-258). This relies on the venue already holding enough balance from prior steps and on the venue's own margin check to reject an under-funded order — consistent with the code's explicit policy that 'a rejection is not a reason to stop' (lines 357-359), but it means a mis-sized order is deliberately submitted rather than scaled to the funds actually made available that step.

findings.summary: Several doc comments explicitly describe how 'the reviewer' will read the code, rather than just documenting the code itself.
findings.detail: config.rs's module doc says the constants are inline 'so the reviewer reads them with the rest of the source' (lines 1-5), and lib.rs's module doc says the limits live in config.rs 'so a depositor reading the page and a reviewer reading the source are looking at the same promises' (lines 14-17). Neither passage tells the reader what rating to give or what to overlook — they justify a design choice (constants over hidden settings) — so this does not read as an attempt to steer the review. It is noted here only because the text explicitly addresses 'the reviewer' by name, and a careful reader should see that mention called out rather than passed over silently.

review.summary: A single long-lived async agent that holds spot BTC and shorts BTC-PERP on one named driver, sizing new carry from a target-deployment fraction of vault value and existing gross exposure, capped by a per-order fraction and a workspace-wide gross-leverage constant, and unwinding/flattening through explicit reduce-only orders when funding drops or a drawdown-from-peak threshold is crossed. Config constants in config.rs are wired through to an SDK Limits struct and to a local cap_by_notional helper for unwinds; the manifest's claims largely trace to these constants. The most consequential issue found is that the drawdown-stop's reference point (the vault's peak value) is kept only in the process's own memory and resets to zero on every restart, contradicting the code's own claim that state loss on restart 'costs a moment and nothing else' — in practice it can cost the entire drawdown-stop guarantee across a restart. A secondary issue is that the paired-order open relies on an unverified assumption that the venue fills both legs atomically, with no explicit check of the returned verdicts. A unit test meant to pin the manifest's claims to the code's constants is itself out of date (asserts a 5% idle buffer against code and manifest that both now say 6%). No evidence of malicious code, hidden date/address-triggered behavior, martingale-style sizing, ML-driven sizing, or author-controlled external feeds was found; the strategy stays within the single declared market throughout.
limits: The shonin-strategy-sdk crate (Limits enforcement inside size_for, the Account/VenueAccount transfer semantics, drivers::account_state/submit, and vault::events) is an external dependency, not part of this submitted project, so the actual numeric enforcement of the leverage, order-size and liquidity claims could not be independently verified beyond trusting the SDK's documented contract.

Which real exchange or liquidity venue the 'local' driver resolves to in production — and therefore the true depth and price-feed trustworthiness of BTC and BTC-PERP the agent would actually trade against — is set by platform-level driver configuration outside this submitted project (shonin.toml only declares an empty `[drivers.local]` section) and was not visible here.

Whether the venue's batched order submission is actually fill-or-nothing (the assumption the paired spot/perp open relies on to avoid directional exposure) is a property of the external driver/venue, not something this source demonstrates.
This is one reading of the code at a point in time, not a proof of safety or of the absence of bugs; no tests were executed and no running build was observed.
